Oglesby says Greenspun obtained court protection and retained the papers. The author interprets the approach as continuing White House interest, but the cited sequence does not prove that the IRS acted on a presidential order.
details: The collection was stored in the Sun’s safe and included documents and tapes from Maheu’s years with Hughes. Oglesby connects it to possible exposure of Nixon–Hughes and CIA–criminal relationships, distinguishing that theory from the earlier claim that the target was material on Muskie.

The documents survived the approach and later assisted Maheu in his libel action, in the book’s account. The timing is what makes the IRS episode significant to Oglesby. Retention of the papers is the concrete outcome; the agency’s precise motivation is not independently established in this extraction.
yankee-irs-greenspun.context: Continuation of the Greenspun document contest during public Watergate hearings.

yankee-reed-letter.summary: NTSB chairman Reed asked the FBI to explain agents’ early and unusual actions after the Flight 553 crash. His letter identified interviews and listening to control-tower tapes before safety investigators acted, and sought records and a clearer division of responsibility. Oglesby uses it to support concerns about investigative overlap, not as proof of sabotage.
details: Reed said the board had discovered actions atypical in its staff’s experience. He requested the purpose, timing, personnel numbers and reports of the FBI inquiry, anticipating questions at congressional oversight hearings.

The letter also proposed a formal interagency understanding to avoid future conflicts. That administrative request matters because it demonstrates concern inside the official investigation, rather than solely from outside critics. The FBI’s later reply supplies a competing explanation that should be read alongside it.
yankee-reed-letter.context: Official evidence of tension between safety and criminal investigators.

yankee-ruckelshaus-letter.summary: Ruckelshaus replied that the FBI investigated potential federal aircraft crimes, initially did not know Dorothy Hunt was aboard and ended its inquiry after finding no apparent violation. He reported roughly fifty agents and first arrival within forty-five minutes. Oglesby questions the scale and timing, but those questions do not disprove the official explanation.
details: The reply invoked jurisdiction over aircraft destruction and crimes aboard aircraft. It explained that an agent was invited by FAA personnel to hear tower recordings and identified a stall warning, and that complete reports were supplied to the NTSB.

Ruckelshaus also named an FBI liaison for future coordination. Oglesby argues that such a large response suggests advance surveillance and that legal authority does not fully explain why resources were mobilized. That is his inference from the response, distinct from the bureau’s statement of what it knew and why it acted.
yankee-ruckelshaus-letter.context: Official answer to Reed’s June 5 inquiry.

yankee-crash-final-report.summary: The NTSB’s final report attributed Flight 553’s crash to crew handling and loss of aircraft control; Oglesby’s appendix challenges its reconstruction. He focuses on the failed flight-data recorder, spoilers, altimeter behavior and cockpit responses. Disagreement with the official explanation does not establish the sabotage mechanism proposed by outside investigators.
details: The appendix summarizes a theory in which distraction by the recorder failure contributed to improper spoiler handling and an aerodynamic stall during the landing sequence. It reviews the cockpit-recording language and the reported aircraft configuration.

Oglesby argues that technical uncertainties and the surrounding political context weaken that conclusion. Elsewhere he acknowledges the weakness of some poisoning claims and reports fire-related cyanide explanations. The timeline should therefore show a published official finding and an attributed critique, rather than substitute a proven covert cause for an allegedly inadequate reconstruction.
yankee-crash-final-report.context: Closes the official aviation inquiry while preserving the book’s unresolved challenge.

yankee-trilateral-founded.summary: Rockefeller formed the Trilateral Commission on Brzezinski’s advice, according to Oglesby, to articulate shared interests among North America, Western Europe and Japan. The author connects it to older establishment networks and resistance to economic nationalism. Those network and faction descriptions are his analytical interpretation rather than proof of a formal parent-body relationship.
details: The passage frames the commission as a response to strains associated with Nixon and Connally’s economic policies and as a forum supporting multinational business interests. Carter and other governors were brought into its discussions as prospective political figures.

Oglesby argues that the institution helped introduce Carter to national foreign-policy circles. He does not describe Carter as merely a puppet; instead, he emphasizes the combination of personal political appeal and organized establishment support. The founding therefore belongs to both institutional history and the book’s interpretation of the post-Nixon transition.
yankee-trilateral-founded.context: Institutional bridge to the Carter administration.
yankee-trilateral-founded.precisionNote: The source supports year precision; placement at the start of that period is a display convention, not an exact day.

yankee-maheu-libel.summary: Maheu won a jury verdict against Hughes over accusations that he was dishonest and had stolen from his employer. Oglesby presents the result as supporting Maheu’s defense after years of investigation failed to substantiate the board’s allegations. The verdict concerns those defamatory charges, not every wider claim about Hughes’s removal or criminal networks.
details: Hughes had made the accusations in a telephone interview during the publicity surrounding Clifford Irving’s false biography. Maheu filed suit in 1972 and obtained the Los Angeles verdict in July 1974, as described by the book.

Oglesby connects the case with the preserved memoranda and tapes in Greenspun’s custody. Their usefulness gives a concrete consequence to the earlier document struggle. The legal victory vindicated Maheu on the issue tried while leaving the author’s questions about the proxy, aides and outside influence separate.
yankee-maheu-libel.context: Later vindication in the aftermath of the Nevada control dispute.
yankee-maheu-libel.precisionNote: The source supports month precision; placement at the start of that period is a display convention, not an exact day.

yankee-carter-team.summary: Carter appointed numerous Trilateral members to senior positions and had chosen Mondale as running mate. Oglesby interprets the concentration as evidence that organized establishment support helped shape the new administration. He allows for Carter’s own populism and coalition-building, so the account should not reduce membership overlap to proof that the commission directed every decision.
details: The passage lists Vance at State, Brown at Defense, Brzezinski as national security adviser, Blumenthal at Treasury and Young at the United Nations, alongside other appointments. Carter’s own description of commission membership emphasizes its value as a foreign-policy learning opportunity.

Oglesby situates the appointments at the end of a cycle he traces from Nixon’s downfall to Carter’s election. That cycle is his explanatory model. The roster supplies specific institutional overlap, while claims about a unified Yankee strategy or hidden management of the presidency require more than the membership list.
yankee-carter-team.context: Endpoint of the book’s Watergate-to-Carter political interpretation.
yankee-carter-team.precisionNote: The source supports year precision; placement at the start of that period is a display convention, not an exact day.
